**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Note for the director: the one thing that most hurts this piece is a Charts and data defect, not a whole-piece one, so I did not file it here. The bar chart's y-axis starts at 2.5% (the baseline at about y=680). As a result the Starter bar (3.1%) looks about a third the height of the Growth bar (4.0%), when the real gap is about 1.3×. The bars tell a much bigger story than the numbers printed on them. The title is a plain label ("Trial to paid conversion by plan"), which is the normal style for a dashboard. So I answered yes to the headline-and-image line and left the mismatch to the data critic.

**What's working.**
- **The page reads as one thing, and every part has a job.** The chart gives the rates. The table at the top right gives the raw counts behind them, which shows that Enterprise's 3.4% rests on only 38 paid accounts. The Definition box says what "converted" means and how open trials are treated. The source line dates the data. None of it is decoration. The numbers also agree: 286/9,210 = 3.1%, 185/5,140 = 3.6%, 118/2,950 = 4.0%, 38/1,120 = 3.4%. The 30 October cutoff also matches the 30-day window for trials started on 30 September.
- **The tone fits the job.** One muted violet, neutral greys and plain sans-serif type make it look calm and trustworthy, which suits an internal analytics page. The active "Conversion" tab uses the same violet as the wordmark, so the page holds together as one family.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **There's one clear place to start, and a clear order after it.** The title "Trial to paid conversion by plan" (about x 48–443, y 95–125) is the largest and heaviest text on the page. It sits top left, so it's read first, and the chart's block of purple bars sits right under it and carries the eye down. The right column is clearly second. Its heading "Trials by plan, Q3 2025" is much smaller (about 15 px against about 26 px), so it doesn't compete with the title. The order is title, then chart, then supporting table and definition, which is right for a page whose job is one comparison.
- **Each level differs in more than size.** The title is bold and near-black, and the subtitle under it is regular weight in mid-grey. The right column's headings ("Trials by plan, Q3 2025", "Definition") are only a little larger than the body text, but they're bold and dark, so they still read as headings. The small table column headers (Plan, Trials, Paid) are bold grey. The axis labels and source line are the smallest and greyest text. Weight and colour mark the fine steps instead of sizes a point apart, as Refactoring UI advises: bolder, not bigger.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I judged this by eye from the whole 1280 × 800 image. It's about one screen, so it didn't need cutting into crops, but the crop script was blocked here, so I couldn't zoom in to check details. The pixel sizes above are estimates. With every line a yes, I had no entries to open.

I'm done. Here is the arrangement report.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No.
   - **Where:** The heaviest thing on the page is the block of four saturated purple bars in the left column (x 108–688, y ~190–680). The right column's content ends at about y 415, after the "Definition" paragraph. Below it, a block of about 464×335 px (x 768–1232, y 415–750) is empty.
   - **What the viewer sees:** All the weight sits low and left, so the lower right looks unfinished rather than deliberately open. It feels like content failed to load, or a panel is missing.
   - **Why:** Weight comes from size, darkness and colour, and a heavy side needs a counterweight (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance").
   - **Fix:** Give the lower right something with weight, or end the right column on purpose.
     - Option 1: move a related element there, such as a "what changed" note or a small companion figure.
     - Option 2: shorten the chart column so the two columns end closer together.
     - Option 3: let the table's rows breathe so the column runs longer.
   - **Label:** Convention. **Weight:** minor. It is a dashboard, and the empty space doesn't stop anyone reading the chart or the table.
2. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?** No.
   - **Where:** The left subtitle's baseline is around y 148 and the right table's header row ("Plan / Trials / Paid") is around y 142. The table rows (y ~176, 216, 256, 296) don't land on anything in the left column. The two column headings also sit at slightly different heights, with cap tops at about y 97 and y 99.
   - **What the viewer sees:** The tops of the two columns almost line up but not quite, so the page reads as two panels placed side by side by eye rather than built on one set of horizontal lines.
   - **Why:** Lines of text should align across columns (see the `references/typography.md` entry "Lines of text align across columns". I couldn't open it because Bash was refused, so this rests on the line's wording).
   - **Fix:** Pick one shared horizontal line and hang both columns from it. The simplest version puts the right heading's baseline on the left title's baseline, or the table header's baseline on the subtitle's.
   - **Label:** Convention. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- **One grid holds the page.** Equal 48 px outer margins hold the page together. Logo, chart title, subtitle and source line all share the x = 48 edge, and the right column's rules and text share x 768–1232, separated from the chart by one clean ~80 px gutter. Nothing looks placed by eye on the horizontal axis.
- **Spacing shows the groups.** Title and subtitle sit tight together, with more space before the chart. The "Definition" heading sits nearer its own paragraph than the table above it, so each group reads without boxes or rules.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** How the two columns reflow at narrower widths. This matters because the lower-right gap may close up or get worse.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (visual weight balances; lines align across columns)

**Section.** Text: applies. The image is a single 1280×800 screen, so I worked from the whole image. The crop script was not run because Bash was refused in this session. At this size it would have printed `no crops` anyway.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One family, one plan.** A single sans family covers everything: the nav, the 26 px or so bold title, the grey 15 px or so subtitle, the 14 px table and definition text, and the 12 px or so axis labels and source line. Weight and grey set the levels apart instead of extra sizes. For example, the table headers "Plan / Trials / Paid" (y≈137) are small, bold and grey rather than a new size. So each size has an obvious job, which is the "bolder, not bigger" approach (Wathan and Schoger, *Refactoring UI*).
- **The numbers line up.** In the table (x≈1100–1232, y≈175–296), "Trials" and "Paid" are right-aligned and the figures look tabular: 9,210, 5,140, 2,950 and 1,120 take the same width. The reader can compare magnitudes down the column at a glance (Bringhurst on figures in tables). Keep this if the numbers ever change length.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Grey small text.** The axis tick labels (x≈68–98), the subtitle (y≈143) and the source line (y≈741) look like a mid grey that clears 4.5:1 on white. To be sure, measure their computed colour against #FFF.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The palette is very small and every colour has a job.** Everything is white and a range of greys except for one purple. The purple shows up in only three places: the four bars, the "Quarry Analytics" wordmark, and the active "Conversion" tab. Because it is that rare, it ties the brand, the current page and the data together, and the eye goes straight to the bars. Nothing else on the page competes for attention.
- **The page still reads in grayscale.** The headline and bar labels are near-black, the bars are a mid-dark purple, the axis and table labels are mid-grey, and the gridlines and table rules are pale grey on white. With the colour taken out, the order of importance would stay the same.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies (one bar chart of conversion by plan, plus a table of trials and paid accounts).

**Findings**
1. **Does each chart keep honest scales: bar axes from zero, even ticks, no unmarked breaks, and one scale for charts that are compared?** No.
   - **Where:** The value axis in the left chart starts at 2.5% (baseline at y≈680), so every bar is cut off at the bottom.
   - **What the viewer sees:** Measured from the baseline, the Growth bar is about 368 px tall (top at y≈312) and the Starter bar about 147 px (top at y≈533). Growth looks 2.5 times Starter, but 4.0% is only 1.29 times 3.1%. That exaggerates the gap about fivefold (Tufte's lie factor ≈ 5). Team (3.6%) also looks nearly twice Starter. A viewer who skims the bars and skips the labels comes away thinking Growth converts far better than the other plans, when all four sit within one percentage point.
   - **Why it matters more here:** The table next to the chart shows that Enterprise rests on 38 paid accounts out of 1,120 trials and Growth on 118 out of 2,950. Gaps of a few tenths of a point between those plans are within ordinary noise, and the truncated bars make that noise look like a real ranking.
   - **Source:** Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, ch. 17.1 "The principle of proportional ink"; Few, "Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design", pitfall 8; Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*, ch. 2 (lie factor).
   - **Fix:** Start the bar axis at zero so bar lengths keep the proportions of the values. To make the small differences readable, switch to dots on a scale that need not start at zero, ideally with a range for each plan given the small counts.
   - **Kind and weight:** Defect, convention. Major.
2. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** No.
   - **Where:** The title "Trial to paid conversion by plan" (y≈110) and the subtitle (y≈143) name the topic and define the measure, but neither says what the data shows. Nothing is annotated on the chart.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The viewer has to work out the point alone, and with the truncated axis the point they reach is "Growth is far ahead". A stated finding would anchor the true size of the gap, for example "All plans convert at 3–4%; Growth leads by under a point".
   - **Source:** The catalog's sources for this are not on the approved list, so this is my judgment.
   - **Fix:** Put the finding in the title or subtitle, with the size of the difference in points.
   - **Kind and weight:** Taste. Minor.
3. **Does each headline number come with a comparison, such as a target, the previous period, or a trend?** No.
   - **Where:** The four rates (bar labels at y≈298–518) are shown for Q3 2025 only. There is no Q2 value, target or trend anywhere on this Conversion page.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** They can compare plans with each other, but they can't tell whether 3.1% for Starter is good, bad, better or worse than last quarter.
   - **Source:** Few, "Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design", pitfall 2.
   - **Fix:** Next to each rate, show the change from the previous quarter or the target, as a small delta or a ghost mark.
   - **Kind and weight:** Convention. Minor.

**What's working.**
- Every bar carries its value as a bold label just above it (y≈298–518), and plan names sit directly under the bars. With a single series in one hue there is no legend to decode. This direct labeling is the right base to keep when the scale changes.
- The table on the right gives the raw trials and paid counts, and its figures check out against the bars (286/9,210 = 3.1%, 185/5,140 = 3.6%, 118/2,950 = 4.0%, 38/1,120 = 3.4%). The definition note and the source line close the obvious questions about what counts as a conversion.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 13 yes, 3 no (honest scales: bar axis starts at 2.5%; title states the finding; headline numbers have a comparison)

Bash was refused, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. I worked from the whole image, which is one screen and fully readable, and read the entries from `references/dataviz.md`.

Walk, Interface (the image is about one screen, 1280×800, so I worked from the whole image. Bash was denied, so I didn't run the crop and entries scripts):

- One primary button, others lower: yes (there are no buttons and no actions to rank)
- Controls look like what they do: yes (the top nav reads as tabs by its position and convention)
- 3:1 non-text contrast: yes (no input borders or icons)
- Hover, pressed and disabled states distinct: yes (only the active tab is shown, and it is distinct)
- Focus indicator: unsure, not shown in a still
- Focus not obscured: yes (no sticky overlays)
- Main content uncovered: yes
- Target size: yes (the nav links are about 60–80 px wide with about 24 px gaps)
- Phone thumb zone: yes (not a phone layout)
- Where the user is: yes (Conversion is bold and dark purple; the source line gives the period)
- Visible way out: yes (no dialog)
- Valid inputs only: yes (no inputs)
- Destructive actions set apart: yes (none)
- Recognition, not recall: yes (rates in the chart, counts in the table, definition on screen)
- Progressive disclosure: yes
- Field labels, natural mapping, one-column form, required markers, error wording, error fixes: yes (no form)
- Empty state: yes (not empty)
- Help near the step: yes (the Definition block sits by the data)
- Shortcuts and filters: no. There is no period picker, plan filter or export anywhere on a dashboard that is fixed to Q3 2025.
- Anticipation: yes
- Conventions: yes
- Audience's words: yes
- Link purpose: yes
- Sensory instructions: yes
- Conceptual model: yes (the tabs run in funnel order)
- Consistency across screens: yes (only one screen is shown)
- Reflow: yes
- Honest choices: yes

**Section.** Interface: applies. The only controls are the top navigation (the brand plus four tabs), so most lines about forms, dialogs and errors are trivially yes.

**Findings**
1. **"Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?"** There is no control on the page for changing the quarter, filtering plans, picking the conversion window or exporting. The header bar (y ≈ 0–60) holds only the tabs, and the period is fixed in the subtitle (48,143), the table title (768,106) and the source line (48,741).
   - **What the viewer experiences:** someone checking conversion on a dashboard usually wants to compare it with last quarter. Here they can't, and nothing tells them whether other periods exist.
   - **Source:** Nielsen heuristic 7, flexibility and efficiency of use.
   - **Fix:** put a period selector, with an optional plan filter, at the right end of the header bar or beside the chart title. Show Q3 2025 as the selected value so the subtitle no longer has to carry the period.
   - Classed as convention. It doesn't apply if this is meant as a fixed, one-off report and not a live dashboard. The tab bar suggests a product, which is why I marked it.
   - **Weight:** minor. The page does its main job, answering "which plan converts best", without it.
   - **Caveat:** Bash was denied, so I couldn't run the entries script, and I didn't open the reference entry for this line. The finding rests on the heuristic itself.

**What's working.**
- The tabs follow the order of the funnel: Acquisition, Conversion, Retention, Revenue. That tells the user how the product's sections relate before they click anything (Norman, conceptual model). Keep that order.
- The active tab, Conversion, is set apart by both weight and color. The cue that says where you are doesn't depend on color alone.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Hover and focus on the nav tabs: whether a focus ring at least 2 px thick with 3:1 contrast appears. Keyboard users need this on the only controls on the page. Check it in a live browser.
- The click area of the tabs: whether it covers the whole header height or only the text. With 24 px gaps it passes either way, but it's worth confirming.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 1 no (shortcuts for frequent actions), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
